newsitem.title: UK: Stricken Branson balloon set to land in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Stricken Branson balloon set to land in Algeria.

text.p: Richard Branson's attempt to be the first person to fly round the world by balloon is due to end in the Algerian desert at daybreak on Wednesday when he will make a forced landing after encountering technical problems.
"They are going to try to land at first light if possible," project director Mike Kendrick told a hastily-arranged news conference at a London hotel.
Earlier, officials had said the British tycoon's balloon would touch down in Algeria at about 0600 GMT.
The officials said they anticipated a calm landing. The lives of Branson and his two co-pilots were not in danger, they added.
"There are no injuries involved, this is purely technical," Kendrick said.

However, what Branson had called "the last great aviation record left on earth" seemed set to end in failure, less than 24 hours after it began on Tuesday at an air base near the ancient Moroccan city of Marrakesh.
Kendrick said Branson had contacted him by radio telephone from the balloon about the technical problem.
"Richard said, typically: 'I am sorry to disappoint you, Mike, we are having to land. We have got a duration problem. Please say sorry to everybody, and we will talk to you later'."
Kendrick could not say exactly what had happened to the balloon.
"The nature of the problem we are still trying to establish. I honestly can't tell you what it is, except that we know it's a ballast versus helium problem," he said.

Kendrick said the British tycoon's Virgin Global Challenger balloon had been as low as 4,000 feet (1,200 metres) earlier on Wednesday and was now at 12,000 feet (3,650 metres). It would pass over mountains and then attempt to land on flat terrain.
In an earlier statement, the control centre in London said the balloon would try to land in an area of Algeria about 50 to 70 miles (80 to 110 km) east of the border with Morocco.
Project officials could not confirm that this was still the intended landing area.
The officials said Algerian rescue services had been alerted.

Political violence has rocked Algeria for the past five years. About 60,000 people have been killed since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
Branson and co-pilots Per Lindstrand and Alex Ritchie were flying in what is believed to be the world's biggest balloon.
"This is one of the most magnificent adventures that anyone could have in their lifetime," Branson told reporters before lift-off.

After taking off, the balloon had headed up into the jetstream they hoped would carry them across North Africa, Saudi Arabia, India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and the United States before landing in Britain after a 24,000-mile (38,600 km) trip expected to take between 14 and 21 days.
Branson had been racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset who is planning a similar round-the-world attempt, launched from Switzerland.
Branson, flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies, has launched an airline and products ranging from condoms to cola and pensions.
The tycoon had to cancel a previous attempt to fly round the globe from Marrakesh last January because of bad weather. He has already crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
